<div class="research-page" id="research-top">
<section class="hero"><div class="wrap"><div class="hero-inner"><div><h1>Chemical tools to <em>see</em><br> and <em>reach</em> inside cells.</h1><p class="hero-copy">We design chemical probes and peptoid transporters to read enzyme activity, visualize cellular environments, and improve intracellular cargo delivery.</p></div><figure class="hero-art research-evidence"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/D6RA06745J" aria-label="Read the peptoid transporter study in RSC Advances"><img src="https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/e9f9/13717953/f9dfc19a15d1/d6ra06745j-f3.webp" width="1599" height="530" alt="Confocal fluorescence microscopy of HeLa cells treated with peptoids 1a–9a: peptoids in green, mitochondria in red, and nuclei in blue; Figure 3 from Shin, Kim et al., RSC Advances, 2026"></a><figcaption><span>PEPTOID TRANSPORTERS · LIVE-CELL IMAGING</span><br>Peptoids in green · mitochondria in red · nuclei in blue<br>Shin, Kim et al. · <em>RSC Advances</em>, 2026 · Fig. 3<br><a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/D6RA06745J">View the study ↗</a> · <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/3.0/">CC BY-NC 3.0</a></figcaption></figure></div><div class="hero-bottom"><b>Drug Target and Biomarker Discovery Laboratory</b></div></div></section>
<nav class="contents" aria-label="Research areas"><div class="wrap"><a href="#protease"><span class="num">01</span>Protease activity<span class="arrow">↘</span></a><a href="#imaging"><span class="num">02</span>Fluorescent imaging<span class="arrow">↘</span></a><a href="#delivery"><span class="num">03</span>Intracellular delivery<span class="arrow">↘</span></a></div></nav>
<div class="wrap"><section class="intro"><h2>Our approach</h2><p>We connect molecular design with measurements in living systems—asking how a molecule’s structure controls what it detects, where it goes, and how it interacts with cells.</p></section>
<section class="area" id="protease"><div class="area-head"><div><div class="area-kicker">01 / Protease activity</div><h2>Chemical readouts<br>of active enzymes.</h2><p class="description">Protease function depends on when and where an enzyme is active. We develop activity-based probes that combine molecular recognition, reactive groups, and fluorescent reporters to investigate active proteases in living cells. Our work spans asparaginyl endopeptidase (AEP) and the HTRA family, with an emphasis on probe reactivity, subtype preference, and subcellular access.</p><div class="tags"><span>Activity-based probes</span><span>AEP / legumain</span><span>HTRA1 &amp; HTRA2</span></div></div><figure class="schematic"><svg viewBox="0 0 480 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Conceptual modular design of an activity-based probe"><g font-family="Arial,sans-serif"><text x="26" y="34" font-size="9" fill="#6b8495" letter-spacing="1.8">A MODULAR CHEMICAL READOUT</text><path d="M88 115h110m48 0h91" stroke="#799bb1" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="77" cy="115" r="28" fill="#70a8d9" fill-opacity=".22" stroke="#367fbb" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="77" cy="115" r="13" fill="#387fb8"/><path d="m176 115 22-16 23 32 22-32 23 16" fill="none" stroke="#426987" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="m345 87 39 28-39 28Z" fill="#d3ad65" stroke="#b18a45" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="m77 148v23m144-23v23m136-23v23" stroke="#9cb1bc"/><text x="77" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#254758">Reporter</text><text x="221" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#254758">Recognition</text><text x="357" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#254758">Reactive group</text><text x="77" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b8495">Optical readout</text><text x="221" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b8495">Target preference</text><text x="357" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b8495">Activity-dependent labeling</text><path d="M28 240h424" stroke="#d4e0e5"/></g></svg><figcaption>Conceptual probe architecture. Specific reporter and recognition elements vary across studies.</figcaption></figure></div><div class="work-label">Selected research</div><div class="papers"><article class="paper"><div class="meta"><span>2017</span><span class="type">Article</span></div><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/C7OB01467H" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Turn-on detection of AEP activity</a></h3><p>A smart probe reports subcellular asparaginyl endopeptidase activity in living cells.</p><div class="citation"><i>Organic &amp; Biomolecular Chemistry</i></div><div class="authors">Hong et al.</div><a class="doi" href="https://doi.org/10.1039/C7OB01467H" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read paper ↗</a></article><article class="paper"><div class="meta"><span>2020</span><span class="type">Article</span></div><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acschembio.0c00279" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Activity-based probes for HTRA proteases</a></h3><p>Live-cell activity measurements include HTRA1 in an AD-like cellular model and mitochondria-targeted labeling of HTRA2.</p><div class="citation"><i>ACS Chemical Biology</i></div><div class="authors">Nam, Song, Eo et al.</div><a class="doi" href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acschembio.0c00279" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read paper ↗</a></article><article class="paper"><div class="meta"><span>2023</span><span class="type">Article</span></div><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bmcl.2023.129259" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Structure–activity relationships for HTRA probes</a></h3><p>Probe design is refined to improve reactivity and preferences among HTRA subtypes.</p><div class="citation"><i>Bioorganic &amp; Medicinal Chemistry Letters</i></div><div class="authors">Song, Lee et al.</div><a class="doi" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bmcl.2023.129259" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read paper ↗</a></article></div></section></div>
<div class="imaging"><div class="wrap"><section class="area" id="imaging"><div class="area-head"><div><div class="area-kicker">02 / Fluorescent imaging</div><h2>Turn cellular environments<br>into visible signals.</h2><p class="description">Fluorogenic molecules translate local chemistry and physical environments into optical signals. We design probes for biological thiols and lipid droplets, and study how molecular structure controls fluorescence responses. These tools support imaging from living cells to tissues; related molecular-rotor chemistry also enables latent-fingerprint visualization.</p><div class="tags"><span>Fluorogenic design</span><span>Lipid droplets</span><span>Live-cell &amp; tissue imaging</span></div></div><figure class="micrograph"><img src="images/paste-2.png" alt="Lipid-droplet images from the current laboratory website, including probe, reference-dye, brightfield, merged and 3D views" width="642" height="255"><figcaption>Lipid-droplet imaging · cellular and subcellular views.<br>Related study: Kim et al., <i>Analytical Chemistry</i> (2024). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.3c05368" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Source paper ↗</a></figcaption></figure></div><div class="work-label">Selected research</div><div class="papers"><article class="paper"><div class="meta"><span>2018</span><span class="type">Article</span></div><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/bkcs.11429" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Biothiol-responsive fluorescence</a></h3><p>A turn-on fluorescent probe enables live-cell imaging of biothiols.</p><div class="citation"><i>Bulletin of the Korean Chemical Society</i></div><div class="authors">Hong et al.</div><a class="doi" href="https://doi.org/10.1002/bkcs.11429" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read paper ↗</a></article><article class="paper"><div class="meta"><span>2022</span><span class="type">Article</span></div><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/D2RA06728E" target="_blank" <div class="wrap"><section class="area delivery" id="delivery"><div class="area-head"><div><div class="area-kicker">03 / Intracellular delivery</div><h2>Design transporters<br>around the cargo.</h2><p class="description">Cellular entry, subcellular localization, and toxicity respond differently to molecular design. We investigate amphipathic peptoids with tunable side chains, charge, and conformation to understand these relationships. From mitochondria-targeting sequences to protein- and nanoparticle-delivery systems, our goal is to balance useful cellular accumulation with compatibility in biological settings.</p><div class="tags"><span>Peptoids &amp;
